chunks: "Fast slew rates buy you speed and cleaner timing.

Edges that traverse the logic threshold quickly leave more of the bit period for setup and hold, there's less jitter and delay variation caused by noise on a slow edge, and in a power switch a fast edge spends less time with high voltage and high current overlapping, so switching loss is lower.
In an amplifier a fast slew rate means less distortion and a wider full-power bandwidth. The cost is everything that grows with dV over dt and dI over dt .
A faster edge has more high-frequency content, so more EMI and higher harmonics where cables and traces radiate well.
It causes larger current spikes and ground bounce, since L di over dt goes up.
It increases crosstalk and makes ringing and overshoot worse because it excites the parasitic L and C.
It needs termination on shorter traces, since reflections matter once the edge is shorter than twice the line delay.
And it may stress the part: overshoot above the supply, or dv over dt turning on a neighboring MOSFET.

Slow edges are the mirror image: quiet and EMI-friendly, but they eat timing margin, increase switching loss in power stages, can create slow-edge sensitivity to noise and cause a lot of short-circuit current in the next stage.
So I'd choose the slowest edge that meets timing, tune with a series resistor or drive-strength setting, and verify on the scope and in EMC."
